H. Tribe is a constitutional law professor at Harvard University and the author of "To End a Presidency: The Power of Impeachment."
President Trump's apparent belief that, as president, he can pardon himself from any wrongdoing has already been ruled out by the Constitution and the courts. But it's worth recalling why that rule exists and why we have it.
In July 1974, the House Judiciary Committee, then chaired by the late Rep. John Conyers (D-Mich.), issued a report on possible impeachment proceedings against President Richard M. Nixon. One of the first things it did was to note that a president can be indicted and tried for any crime, but that he cannot be pardoned for that crime. Later, in October 1974, the House Judiciary Committee issued a final report on impeachment, at which point the Constitution's pardon clause was examined again. It was explained that no one can pardon himself.
The clearest provision in the Constitution is Article II, Section 4: "
sampled: By now, the Trump administration's apparent belief that, as president, he can pardon himself from wrongdoing has been ruled out by the Constitution and the courts. It is useful to remember why this rule is what it is. The pardon clause of the Constitution was examined again in a report by the House Judiciary Committee in October 1974. The report, prepared by John Conyers, D-Mich., a member of the Committee at the time, started with the observation that a president can be indicted and tried for a crime, but cannot be pardoned for the same crime. The clearest provision of the Constitution is Article II, paragraph 4: “No person shall be privileged to pardon any person except the President; and no person shall be privileged to pardon any person from punishment for any crime except the President.” The report then explained that no one can pardon himself.

There’s a lot of debate amongst analysts about the right way to identify “business intelligence” (BI) solutions for a company. While analyst opinions vary, the truth is there are at least three types of BI buyers.
The traditional BI buyer is a large enterprise, enterprise system integrator, or managed service provider (MSP). These companies have a strong IT infrastructure and need a way to get their data into the “cloud” and have that data “stored” in the cloud. Many of these companies also have a very large volume of data that needs to be analyzed. The traditional BI solutions have a great big “data lake” that can store all that data.
The next type of BI buyer is the SMB or small to medium size business (SMB) buyer. This buyer doesn’t have a lot of IT resources and has a smaller data volume. They also have a greater need to be able to �
sampled: The BI buyer is usually a large company, a systems integrator or an MSP. The views of the industry analysts are somewhat different, but there are at least three types of buyers of BI solutions. These companies are large and have an extremely large amount of data that must be analyzed. The traditional BI solutions have a large "data lake" that can store all that data. These companies have a solid IT foundation and need to be able to transfer their data to the cloud and store it there. These companies also have a higher need to be able to retrieve their data from the cloud. The next type of BI buyer is the SMB buyer, which is the buyer for small and medium-sized businesses.
